title: Patterns and architecture
summary: Observer, strategy and composition, factories and single instances, and dependency inversion, read and written as code.

misconceptions.description: Believes a listener that subscribes late also receives the messages sent before it subscribed.
Believes that when several functions are registered or passed in, only one of them (the first or the latest) is ever called.
Believes removing one listener empties the whole list of listeners.
Believes a Set limits how often its stored functions can be called.
Believes combining several abilities in one object needs a class hierarchy with extends.
Believes handing an object to another variable, function or class copies it, so writes are not seen by the original.
Believes a function that hands out a single instance builds a new object on every call.
Believes a factory returns the class itself rather than an instance of it.
Believes every factory call with the same argument returns the same object.
Believes pushing onto an array replaces what the array already holds.
Believes using a different helper means editing the function that uses it.
Believes a function that receives a helper still uses its own fixed one, so the passed function cannot change the result.
Believes joining rules in a different order gives the same result.
Believes a joined function runs its last rule first.

conceptCard.title: Observer: publish and subscribe
conceptCard.body: A subject keeps a list of functions. Subscribing adds a function to the list, and publishing calls every function in it with the same value. Unsubscribing removes one function from the list. The publisher does not know who listens. A function that subscribes later hears only later messages.

conceptCard.title: Pass the rule in, combine small pieces
conceptCard.body: A strategy is a function you pass in to decide how one step is done. The surrounding code stays the same while the function changes. Composition builds bigger behaviour by combining small functions or objects instead of extending a class.

conceptCard.title: Factories build, a single instance is reused
conceptCard.body: A factory is a function that builds and returns objects, so callers do not choose the class themselves. A single instance is built once and reused: the first call creates it and every later call returns the same object.

conceptCard.title: Receive what you need
conceptCard.body: Code depends on an abstraction when it receives what it needs as a parameter instead of reaching for a fixed choice. You can then pass a real helper or a fake one. The caller decides, and the function itself does not change.

items.prompt: A hand-written emitter notifies its listeners. What does this program print?

options.feedback: You thought the bay listener hears the first emit. Check where line 8 sits compared with the emit on line 7.
Right. The first emit reaches only the pier listener. The second emit reaches both, and the bay listener negates 5.
You thought only the newest listener is called. Look at line 4: how many functions does the loop call?

items.explanation: emit calls every function stored in subs at that moment. The first emit finds one listener. The second finds two, because the bay listener subscribed in between. Nothing replays old messages to a late subscriber.
hints: Look at where line 8 sits compared with the two emit calls.
emit notifies only the listeners that are registered when it runs.
Count how many listeners exist at the first emit, then at the second.
items.author: claude-fable-5-2/unit-author

items.prompt: Which statement explains why the second send prints bb and no plain b?

options.text: off() empties the whole Set, so no listener is left for the second send.
options.feedback: You thought off() removes every listener. If it did, the second send would print nothing, yet the prompt says it prints bb.

options.text: A Set calls each stored function only once, so the second send reaches only one listener.
options.feedback: twice runs on both sends, so a Set does not limit calls. forEach calls every stored function on every send.

options.text: on returns a function that deletes only this listener from the Set, so later sends skip show but still reach twice.
options.feedback: Right. Calling the returned function removes show from subs, while twice stays in the Set.

items.explanation: Subscribing returns an unsubscribe function that closes over fn. Calling it deletes that one listener from the Set. The second forEach finds only twice, so it prints bb and no plain b.
hints: Compare the two forEach lines and look at what happens between them.
An unsubscribe function undoes exactly one subscription.
Ask which function is removed by line 11, and what the Set holds afterwards.
items.author: claude-fable-5-2/unit-author

items.prompt: off(bell) should remove only the bell listener, so the program prints L. Tap the buggy line and pick the fix.

options.feedback: Every function is truthy, so filter keeps all of them and the bell is still notified.
This removes the lamp listener too, so nothing prints.
Right. filter keeps every function except the one being removed.

items.explanation: filter keeps the elements for which the test is true. The test x === fn keeps only the function to remove and drops everyone else. To unsubscribe one listener, keep every function that is different from it.
hints: Read the test inside filter on line 4 and ask what it keeps.
filter keeps the elements whose test is true.
Line 4 keeps the wrong group of functions; decide which group off should keep.
items.author: claude-fable-5-2/unit-author

items.prompt: Write the body of replay(commands). Commands: 'on:name', 'off:name', 'pub:message'. Return an array with one comma-joined text per pub: message, then current subscribers in order, each once.
items.explanation: Keep a Set of subscribers. An on adds a name, an off deletes only that name, and a pub records the message with every name in the Set at that moment. The Set also ignores a second subscription by the same name.
hints: You need a collection of the names that are listening right now.
Subscribing and unsubscribing change the collection; publishing only reads it.
Split each command at the colon, then add, delete, or loop over the collection depending on the first part.
items.author: claude-fable-5-2/unit-author

items.prompt: chain joins two rules into one. What does this program print?

options.feedback: Right. chain runs its first rule, then hands the result to its second rule, so swapping the arguments swaps the order.
The order matters here: dividing then subtracting is not the same as subtracting then dividing.
You thought chain runs the second rule first. Read line 4: which function does the argument n go into first?

items.explanation: chain returns a function that applies first, then second to that result. chain(half, minus) gives 50 / 2 = 25, then 25 - 5 = 20. chain(minus, half) gives 50 - 5 = 45, then 45 / 2 = 22.5.
hints: Work out each call separately, starting with the rule it receives first.
chain applies its first rule to the number and its second rule to that result, so the argument order sets the step order.
In the first call half runs before minus; in the second call minus runs before half.
items.author: claude-fable-5-2/unit-author

items.prompt: Which statement explains how duck gets both of its moves?

options.text: duck extends a parent class that defines swim and fly, so each new mix of moves needs a new subclass.
options.feedback: You thought a parent class defines the moves. Search the program for the word extends.

options.text: make copies the moves array, so pushing another function into it later would not change duck.go().
options.feedback: make stores the same array it was given, not a copy. go reads it every time it runs, so a later push would show up.

options.text: make builds duck from the move functions it is given, so any mix of moves works without a class hierarchy.
options.feedback: Right. Behaviour comes from the functions passed in, and a different list gives a different object.

items.explanation: Composition builds an object by combining behaviours it is handed. make stores the list of move functions, and go runs each of them. A different array gives a different duck, and no parent class is needed.
hints: Look at what make receives on line 6 and what it does with it.
Composition combines small pieces instead of extending a parent.
Ask where swim and fly come from, and whether any class defines them.
items.author: claude-fable-5-2/unit-author

items.prompt: pick returns the rule for a mode, or the bus rule if unknown, so the program prints 27 and 6. Tap the buggy line and pick the fix.

options.feedback: fare.bus always exists, so || never looks at fare[m] and every mode gets the same rule.
&& keeps the right side whenever the left side exists, so a known mode would be replaced by the bus rule.
Right. The brackets read the key stored in m, and || falls back to the bus rule when that key is missing.

items.explanation: fare.m looks for a property literally named m, which does not exist, so || always falls back to the bus rule. Square brackets use the value of m as the key, so fare[m] finds the taxi rule, and || still covers an unknown mode.
hints: Look at how line 6 finds the rule inside fare.
A dot reads a fixed name; square brackets read a name stored in a variable.
The key must come from the parameter m, and the bus rule must stay as the fallback.
items.author: claude-fable-5-2/unit-author

items.prompt: compose(f, g) should run g first and then f. Complete line 2 so the program prints 7.

options.feedback: Right. The outer call is the second step, which is f here.
Right. The inner call is the first step, which is g here.
x holds a number, and a number cannot be called, so the program fails.
n exists only inside the small helper functions, so using it here fails.

items.explanation: compose returns a function that applies g to x and then f to that result. With half as g, 10 becomes 5, and fee as f makes it 7. Swapping the two would add the fee first and give 6.
hints: Check which function should run first for compose(fee, half).
A call written inside another call's parentheses runs first, and its result feeds the outer call.
The inner blank is the first step; the outer blank is the step that follows.
items.author: claude-fable-5-2/unit-author

items.prompt: get hands out a shared desk object. What does this program print?

options.feedback: You thought get builds a new object on every call. Look at line 3: when does ?? use its right side?
You thought writing through a leaves the shared object unchanged. Line 7 assigns to a.visits: ask which object that changes.
Right. Both calls return the same object, so the change made through a shows through b.

items.explanation: The first call to get creates the object and stores it in desk. The second call finds desk already set and returns the same object. So a and b are one object, and the 4 written through a is read through b.
hints: Follow what desk holds at each of the two calls to get.
?? keeps the left side unless it is null or undefined.
Ask whether the second call builds a new object or returns the stored one.
items.author: claude-fable-5-2/unit-author

items.prompt: Which statement about make is correct for this program?

options.text: make returns the class itself, and go() is then called on that class.
options.feedback: You thought make hands back the class. Check line 8: is there a new, and what does line 9 call go on?

options.text: make keeps one instance per kind, so calls with the same name return the same object.
options.feedback: You thought make caches instances. Look for a variable in make or outside it that stores an instance.

options.text: make turns a name into an instance, so callers never write new themselves.
options.feedback: Right. The choice of class lives in one place, and callers ask for a kind by name.

items.explanation: A factory centralises which class gets built. make looks the class up by name and calls new itself, so its callers only handle the finished objects. Each call returns a new instance of the chosen class.
hints: Look at who writes new in this program.
A factory function builds and returns instances on behalf of its caller.
Check whether the callers on lines 9 and 10 write new or pass only a name.
items.author: claude-fable-5-2/unit-author

items.prompt: getJar should create the jar once and then reuse it, so the program prints 2. Tap the buggy line and pick the fix.

options.feedback: The left side is never null, so ?? always keeps it and a new jar is built on every call.
jar starts as null, and && then stays null. The first call returns null and reading cookies from it fails.
Right. The jar is built only while jar is still null; later calls return the stored one.

items.explanation: Line 3 builds a new object on every call, so each increment lands on a jar that is thrown away and the last call sees a fresh 0. Building the object only while jar is null makes all calls share one jar.
hints: Check what line 3 does on the second and third call.
A single instance is created once and then returned every time.
Line 3 must build the object only under a condition on jar; decide which side holds the stored jar.
items.author: claude-fable-5-2/unit-author

items.prompt: Write the body of firstOrRepeat(keys). A key's instance is built once. Return an array with one answer per key, in order: 'new' for its first request, 'same' for later ones.
items.explanation: Remember every key you have already built in a Map or Set. If the key is stored, the instance exists and the answer is same; otherwise store it and answer new. Comparing only with the previous key forgets older ones.
hints: You need a memory of every key that has been requested so far.
A cached factory builds on a miss and reuses on a hit.
Check the memory for each key; add the key on a miss.
items.author: claude-fable-5-2/unit-author

items.prompt: Notes receives its store from outside. What does this program print?

options.feedback: You thought add changes a copy. Look at line 3: what does the constructor store?
push adds to the end of the array and does not replace what is already there.
Right. Notes uses the fake store it was given, so the new note lands in the array that fake names.

items.explanation: The constructor stores a reference to the array passed in. add pushes onto that same array. Because fake and this.store are one object, the caller sees the new note. The class never creates a store of its own.
hints: Follow the array passed on line 10 into the constructor.
A dependency passed in is the same object the caller holds.
Ask what push does to an array that is shared by two names.
items.author: claude-fable-5-2/unit-author

items.prompt: Which statement explains the two printed lines?

options.text: withFee receives its fee rule as a parameter, so the caller picks the rule and withFee itself never changes.
options.feedback: Right. withFee depends on whatever function it is given, not on one fixed rule.

options.text: withFee must be edited to switch from percent to flat, because the rule is chosen inside it.
options.feedback: You thought switching rules means editing withFee. Compare lines 6 and 7: do they call the same withFee?

options.text: withFee has one fixed fee of its own, and the function passed in only changes how the result looks.
options.feedback: You thought the helper inside withFee is fixed. Read lines 3 to 5: where does fee come from?

items.explanation: withFee does not choose its fee rule; it receives one. The caller passes percent or flat, so the same code gives 110 and 105. Receiving the helper lets a fake replace the real one.
hints: Compare the last two lines: only the second argument differs.
A function that receives what it uses depends on an abstraction, not on one fixed helper.
Ask which line decides the fee rule that withFee uses.
items.author: claude-fable-5-2/unit-author

items.prompt: Alert should use the send function it receives, so the program prints fake ann. Tap the buggy line and pick the fix.

options.feedback: mail is a function, so it is always truthy and || never reaches send.
This calls send once with mail as its argument and stores the text it returns, not a function.
Right. The object now keeps the function it was given, and the default mail applies only when nothing is passed.

items.explanation: The constructor takes send but stores mail, so the injected function is never kept and fire always uses the fixed helper. Storing the parameter lets the caller choose the behaviour, and the default still covers a missing argument.
hints: Compare what line 5 stores with the parameter declared on line 4.
A dependency passed in is useless unless the object keeps and uses it.
Line 4 gives the parameter a default; line 5 must use that parameter.
items.author: claude-fable-5-2/unit-author

items.prompt: report receives now, mark and out functions. Fill all three blanks so the program prints *9.

options.feedback: Right. The first parameter is called with no arguments and gives 9.
Right. The second parameter receives the clock result and adds the star.
Right. The wrapper keeps lines as the array the push is called on.
push is detached from lines here, so it has no array to add to when out calls it.
This passes the number 9, and report then tries to call a number, which fails.

items.explanation: report calls its first argument for a value, passes that to its second, and hands the result to its third. Passing the functions themselves works, but lines.push alone loses its array, so the third needs a wrapper.
hints: Look at which parameter is called with no arguments on line 2.
Pass functions, not their results, and remember a method taken from an object loses that object.
The first blank gives a value, the second changes it, and the third must still reach lines.
